materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.006 S20 Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

notes.summary: The Spring 2020 edition opens with the course's core contract: an algorithm is a finite procedure with a proof of correctness and an analysis of running time. You review the asymptotic language (Big-O, Theta) and meet the course's three big families: algorithmic thinking, data structures, and graph algorithms. This semester's recorded lectures by Devadas, Demaine, and Soloviev are the newest full-video edition of 6.006 available.
notes.focus: Rewrite your 61B asymptotics notes in 6.006's notation before starting PS1 — the courses share vocabulary, but 6.006 uses it more precisely.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.006 S20 Lecture 2: Data Structures and Dynamic Arrays

notes.summary: Sets and sequences as the two interface families, and the data structures that implement them. The dynamic array (your 61B ArrayDeque) gets its amortized analysis done rigorously: table doubling gives O(1) amortized append. The interface/implementation split is 6.006's way of thinking about every structure that follows.
notes.focus: Prove amortized O(1) append via the bank/potential argument in your own words. This proof template returns for splay trees and hash resizing.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.006 S20 Lecture 3: Sets and Sorting

notes.summary: Sorting as the entry to algorithm design: comparison sorts, the permutation sort's n! lower bound, and mergesort's divide-and-conquer recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n). You also meet insertion sort and the decision-tree view of why comparison sorting can't beat n log n.
notes.focus: Solve the merge sort recurrence with a recursion tree, not the master theorem. Trees make the O(n log n) obvious; the theorem only certifies it.

notes.summary: Hashing buys expected O(1) set operations by trading order for speed. Universal hashing — choosing a hash family at random — is the theory that makes the guarantee hold against adversarial inputs, and chaining resolves collisions. This is the deeper version of what 61B showed you: here you prove the adversary can't win.
notes.focus: Compute the expected lookup cost for a table at load factor alpha, then explain to yourself why randomizing the hash function matters only against adversaries.

notes.summary: Beating the comparison bound by exploiting structure: counting sort runs in O(n + u) when keys are small integers, and radix sort pipelines counting sort per digit for O(nk). The lesson generalizes — lower bounds apply to a model, and changing the model (word-level operations) changes the game.
notes.focus: Implement radix sort over counting sort for 32-bit integers and reason about the k passes. Then ask: why doesn't this violate the decision-tree theorem?

lessons.title: Binary Trees: BSTs and AVL Balance

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.006 S20 Lecture 7: Binary Trees Part 2: AVL

notes.summary: Binary search trees implement ordered sets with logarithmic operations — IF they stay balanced. Lecture 6 (reading) covers BST mechanics; this lecture builds AVL trees, whose height invariant triggers rotations on insert. Rotations are the surgical move that every balanced-tree variant (B-trees, red-black) reuses with different bookkeeping.
notes.focus: Insert a sorted sequence into an AVL by hand and watch each rotation fire. Then do the same insertions into a plain BST — the contrast is the entire point.

notes.summary: The binary heap implements a priority queue with O(log n) insert and delete-min and O(1) find-min, all in a flat array. Building a heap from n items bottom-up costs O(n) — a classic surprise — and heapsort falls out for free. Heaps return as the engine of Dijkstra in a few lessons.
notes.focus: Prove the O(n) build-heap bound by summing per-level work. The series sums to a constant — seeing that sum is a rite of passage.

notes.summary: Graph traversal, the course's pivot point. BFS (lecture 9, reading) explores level by level and computes shortest unweighted paths; DFS (this lecture) dives deep first, with white/gray/black timestamps that expose edge classification: tree, back, forward, cross. Cycle detection and topological sort come free from DFS's structure.
notes.focus: Run DFS on a digraph and label every edge type. Then find the topological order from postorder numbers — one algorithm, two products.

notes.summary: Weighted shortest paths, in order: the relaxation framework (lecture 11, reading), Bellman-Ford's general-but-slow O(VE) (lecture 12), and Dijkstra's heap-driven O(E log V) for nonnegative weights. The priority queue from the heap lesson becomes the engine — course material compounding exactly as designed.
notes.focus: Trace Dijkstra on a small graph where a negative edge would break it. One hand-trace of the failing case cures 'when can I use Dijkstra' forever.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.006 S20 Lecture 15: Dynamic Programming Part 1

notes.summary: The course's crown jewel: dynamic programming. The SRTBOT recipe — Subproblem, Relate, Topological order, Base case, Original problem, Time — turns exponential recursion into polynomial tabulation. Fibonacci and DAG paths are the worked examples; the memoization vs bottom-up distinction is drawn carefully.
notes.focus: Apply SRTBOT on paper to a problem you've only solved recursively. Write the RELATE line first — it is the theorem; everything else is bookkeeping.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.006 S20 Lecture 16: Dynamic Programming Part 2

notes.summary: DP on strings and sequences: longest common subsequence and longest increasing subsequence show suffix-subproblem design, and coin-change shows parenthesization-style ranges. The pattern to internalize: identify what varies (suffix? pair of suffixes? interval?) and define subproblems over exactly that.
notes.focus: Build the full LCS table for two short strings and recover the actual subsequence by walking backwards. The table is the algorithm; reading it is the skill.

notes.summary: Checkpoint on the first two-thirds: data structures, sorting, hashing, trees, heaps, and graph algorithms. Work the two quiz-review videos pause-first — commit to an answer before the instructor solves it. The remaining week covers advanced DP, so fluency here compounds immediately.
notes.focus: Keep a wrong-answer log across both reviews. Every miss maps to one lecture — rewatch only those instead of everything.

notes.summary: The finale opens the door to the theory that follows: lecture 19 (reading) sketches complexity classes and reductions — the P vs NP question that 6.046J formalizes next. The review lecture sweeps the whole toolkit. Your takeaway artifact: one page mapping each problem type to its algorithm and cost, which becomes your 6.046J cheat sheet.
notes.focus: Build that one-page cost table from memory. If a cell is blank, that lecture is your review target — the table is the course.
